fatal_errors: The proposed thermally activated cross-slip of sessile super-dislocations contradicts the target mechanism: yielding initiates through dislocation nucleation at vacancy clusters/disordered atoms and subsequent Shockley-partial slip.

Cross-slip presupposes mobile pre-existing dislocations, while the hypothesis specifies a nearly dislocation-free crystal and does not explain the first carrier nucleation responsible for the yield-point stress drop.

The strain-rate range of 10^-4 to 10^2 s^-1 does not reconstruct the molecular-dynamics regime of 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1, so the asserted rate insensitivity is being extrapolated across many unsupported orders of magnitude.

The required orientation anisotropy is not addressed: the relevant comparison is among <110>, <1-12>, and <-111>, with maximum yield stress along <-111>; merely fixing [001] or [111] cannot establish this constraint.
No evidence is supplied for high Peierls friction, chemical short-range order, super-dislocations, or cross-slip being rate limiting in this FCC alloy.
explanation: The hypothesis recognizes the FCC single-crystal setting, temperature-induced yield softening, weak yield-rate sensitivity, increased importance of crystal orientation, and absence of an FCC-to-BCC transformation. Its diffraction-based falsification test is useful because emergent BCC reflections at yield would directly challenge a slip-only interpretation, although diffraction should be complemented by CNA/DXA or TEM identification of Shockley partials and stacking-fault-induced HCP-like regions. The central mechanism is nevertheless incompatible with the target: yield begins by nucleation at vacancy/disordered sites, followed by 1/6<112> Shockley partials and intrinsic/extrinsic stacking faults, not collective cross-slip of super-dislocations. The generated study also substitutes laboratory strain rates for the specified MD rates and omits the decisive orientation series and <-111> maximum. Thus it is novel but unsupported rather than a valid reconstruction.
